Set up something fun this week: my AI assistant Misato (Grok Bot) can now use my Mac mini's Mail, Messages, Calendar, Contacts and Maps remotely. All read-only, all through MCP.

The core is iMCP, a macOS app that exposes Apple's apps as MCP tools. Its imcp-server speaks stdio, which is great locally, but my assistant lives in the cloud, so I needed a real HTTP endpoint. Here's the chain:

Grok Bot connector (HTTPS + Bearer token)
-> Tailscale Funnel (public HTTPS on my tailnet)
-> Caddy on 127.0.0.1:8001, checks the token
-> supergateway on :8000 (stdio to streamable HTTP)
-> imcp-server -> Mail, Messages, Calendar, Contacts, Maps

Caddy is the bouncer. Without a valid Bearer token you get a 401, both locally and over the Funnel. With one, MCP initialize comes back clean and Misato sees the tools. My work calendar stays on my iPhone, which she reads separately, and she flags conflicts between the two in my morning rundown.

Next up are launchd persistence and locking the bridge to localhost. If you've got a Mac sitting around, iMCP + supergateway + Caddy + Tailscale Funnel turns out to be a surprisingly small amount of glue!

note_tweet.text:
YOUR FIRST GROK BOT SHOULD BE BORING ENOUGH TO TRUST.

most people see “AI teammate” and immediately design an org chart: a stack of roles, every available tool, and a vague mission to “run the business.”

it looks ambitious. it is also impossible to debug when the output goes wrong.

the smarter first move is narrower. give one Grok Bot one workflow with a visible finish line. every morning, it reviews unread customer emails, groups them by urgency, researches the missing context, and prepares replies for approval.

then judge the handoff, not the performance.

did it use the right sources? 
did it preserve context?
did it return at the right decision point? 
did it remove more work than it created?

if it fails, the scope is small enough to correct once and test again. if it works, you now have a repeatable unit that can expand without pretending to be an entire company.

the first useful Grok Bot will not feel like a new department.

it will feel like one task you stopped carrying.

Hey @termix_ai builders 🤖

AI agents are getting more powerful, but can we trust them with real money? 👀

Seeing four data leaks in one day makes this question even more important. As AI agents become part of our daily workflows, security, accountability, and payment protection cannot be ignored.

This is one reason I’m paying attention to what @termix_ai is building.

TermiX is approaching agent commerce with a structured workflow:

🔹 Escrow — Keep payment secured while the job is in progress.
🔹 Deliver — Let the agent submit its completed work.
🔹 Challenge — Allow issues to be raised when something goes wrong.
🔹 Settle — Finalize payment through the settlement process.

Simple steps, but an important idea behind them: AI agents should not just be able to perform tasks. There should also be a clear process for handling work, payments, and potential disputes.

Another interesting part is the ability to connect agent workflows with tools like Grok Bot, Claude, Dot, and Muse through TermiX Agent Skills.

The bigger picture goes beyond AI generating answers. Imagine agents that can find jobs, complete useful work, submit deliverables, and receive payment through a defined process.

That’s where the agent economy starts becoming more practical.

Of course, no system is completely risk-free. The real test will be how reliably these mechanisms work in real-world situations.

I believe the future of AI agents depends not only on what they can do, but also on how safely and transparently they can do it.

Intelligence gets an agent started. Trust is what helps the economy grow. 🤖

#TermiX #AIAgents #AgentEconomy
